drills.q: Why can two threads running counter++ lose an increment?
options: It is three operations, and both can load before either stores
The compiler reorders the increment past the store
The cache line is shared and one write is dropped
Integer overflow wraps the value
drills.why: Both load 7, both compute 8, both store 8. One increment disappeared and nothing anywhere reported an error.

drills.q: What does the lock prefix do on a modern processor?
options: Takes exclusive ownership of the cache line for the duration
Asserts a signal that stops every other core using the memory bus
Disables interrupts until the instruction completes
Flushes the store buffer
drills.why: The name is historical. Early processors did lock the bus, which was correct and extremely expensive. No bus is locked now; one line is owned.

drills.q: What dominates the cost of an atomic operation?
options: Contention, meaning how many other cores want the same line
The atomicity itself
The memory fence it implies
The width of the operand
drills.why: Uncontended it is tens of cycles. On a line several cores are fighting over it is hundreds, and it gets worse as you add cores.

drills.q: What does a failed compare and swap return?
options: Failure, plus the value it actually found, so the retry can use it
Failure only
The value it would have written
It blocks until it can succeed
drills.why: That convention is what makes the retry loop work. Without it a loop would try the same stale value forever.

drills.q: What does a compare-and-swap retry loop actually do?
options: Restarts after losing a race, which means somebody else made progress
Spins waiting for a resource to be released
Backs off exponentially before trying again
Blocks the thread until the value changes
drills.why: That is the difference between lock free and a spin lock, and it is why the system advances whenever anybody wins.

options: A value changed to something else and back, so the comparison succeeds and the assumption is wrong
Two threads swapping the same value simultaneously
A compare and swap that succeeds on a stale cache line
A retry loop that never terminates
drills.why: Compare and swap checks that a location still holds a value. It cannot check that the location never changed.

drills.q: Why is ABA harmless for a counter and dangerous for a pointer?
options: A node can be freed, reallocated and land at the same address, so the structure was rebuilt underneath you
Pointers are wider than counters
Counters are always accessed with relaxed ordering
It is equally dangerous for both
drills.why: The standard repair is a tag that increments on every change, which is why x86-64 has a sixteen-byte compare and swap.

drills.q: Why does the processor reorder a store and a later load?
options: The store goes into a buffer and drains later, so the load can complete first
To hide branch misprediction latency
Because loads have higher priority in the scheduler
It does not; only the compiler reorders
drills.why: It preserves what a single thread can observe about its own execution. It does not preserve what another thread sees.

drills.q: Which reordering does x86-64's total store order permit?
options: A store followed by a load of a different address
Any pair
Two stores
Two loads
drills.why: That one entry is the whole list, which is why a great deal of incorrectly synchronised code happens to work on x86.

drills.q: Why do memory ordering bugs turn up when porting to ARM?
options: ARM permits almost any reordering, so a bug that x86 hid becomes visible
ARM has weaker cache coherence
ARM atomics are not sequentially consistent by default
The compiler optimises differently for ARM
drills.why: The bug was always there. It is the most common way an ordering bug is discovered, and it was never about the new architecture.

drills.q: Two threads each store to one variable then load the other. Can both loads return zero?
options: Yes, on x86, because each store is still in its own core's buffer
No, that appears in no interleaving
Only on ARM
Only without atomics
drills.why: It appears in no interleaving of the source and the hardware produces it anyway. That is the case a fence exists to forbid.

options: Atomicity, and nothing about ordering
Ordering within one thread but not between threads
That the operation is visible before the next one starts
Nothing at all
drills.why: It is right for a statistics counter nobody reads until the end, and wrong for almost everything else.

drills.q: What does a release store paired with an acquire load give you?
options: Everything the writer did before the release is visible to a reader that sees that value
A single global order all threads agree on
Atomicity of the store
A guarantee that the reader will see the value promptly
drills.why: This is the ordering a mutex provides, and it is what most code actually needs.

drills.q: What is a data race in C or C++?
options: Undefined behaviour, which the compiler may assume does not happen
A stale or torn read
A performance problem, not a correctness one
Defined behaviour with an unspecified value
drills.why: A loop polling a non-atomic flag can be turned into a loop that reads it once, because nothing in the program is allowed to change it. The fix is not volatile, which says nothing about ordering or atomicity between threads.

drills.q: What is the difference between lock free and wait free?
options: Lock free means some thread progresses; wait free means every thread finishes in bounded steps
Lock free uses atomics and wait free uses fences
They are the same property under two names
Wait free permits blocking and lock free does not
drills.why: An individual thread can retry indefinitely under a lock-free algorithm, which is why almost everything called lock free is not wait free, and why the reason to choose it is usually robustness rather than throughput.
